findings.title: f32/f64 claim is false — GPU `TickResult` will break the wire contract
findings.description: The doc asserts "`export_positions()` and `export_velocities()` return f64 arrays (Quadrants upcasts on download). The `TickResult` therefore carries f64." This is factually wrong against the code it reuses. In `src/migratory/bench/backends/quadrants_fused_state.py`, `export_positions()` and `export_velocities()` are annotated `-> NDArray[np.float32]` and explicitly end with `.astype(np.float32, copy=False)`; there is no upcast. `TickResult.from_quadrants_fields()` (`src/migratory/engine/tick_result.py`) passes the arrays through unchanged, so the GPU path produces f32 arrays. The slice does not list changing any export method in its "GpuAgentState Changes" or "Files Changed" sections — it adds only `setup_from_server()` and `upload_positions()`. Downstream, `protocol.serialize_state_update()`/`serialize_snapshot()` call `.tobytes()` on those arrays while `deserialize_message()` hard-codes `<f8` reads (`count*2` f64s), and `bounds_enforcement` writes f64-oriented logic; f32 arrays would emit truncated/misaligned frames. This directly contradicts success criterion A3 ("same shape and dtype contract as the CPU path … zero changes downstream") at line 328. The design must specify an explicit upcast to f64 (at export or in the wrapper) or revise the contract claim — as written it cannot satisfy A3 without corrupting the wire.

findings.title: Bounds sync-back is position-only; REFLECT velocities and SOFT enforcement are lost
findings.description: The described sync-back uploads **positions only** (`notify_positions_modified(positions)` → `upload_positions()`). But `apply_bounds_policy()` for `REFLECT` mutates **velocities** too (`_apply_reflect` flips outward velocity components in `src/migratory_server/bounds_enforcement.py`); those flips are never uploaded, so GPU agents keep pushing outward and get re-clamped every tick — reflection is broken. For `SOFT`, `apply_bounds_policy()` is an explicit no-op — soft bounds are applied by `WorldBoundsRepulsor`, which `build_forces()` injects as a CPU `BulkForce` (`src/migratory_server/force_builder.py`). The fused GPU kernel has no repulsor, so there is nothing to sync back and no soft enforcement occurs at all; the "same sync-back pattern" for SOFT is inapplicable. Both contradict A4 ("all four BoundsPolicy variants produce valid … positions"). Either add velocity sync-back and a GPU repulsor (or reject SOFT for the `quadrants` backend), or narrow A4.

findings.title: Two sources of truth: CPU `entity_manager.state` is never updated on the GPU path
findings.description: On the CPU path, `tick()` mutates `AgentState` in place, so `entity_manager.state` stays current each tick. On the GPU path nothing writes downloaded state back into it — `GpuSimulationDriver.step()` returns a fresh `TickResult` from GPU fields. The design never addresses the consequences: (1) `make_snapshot_builder()` in `src/migratory_server/clients.py` builds snapshots from `em.state`/`em.count`, so a client connecting mid-run receives stale spawn-time state; (2) `sync_from_entity_manager()` ("Re-upload CPU state after spawn/despawn," line 162) would upload that same stale CPU state, potentially resetting all existing GPU agents to spawn positions; (3) `GpuAgentState` fields are allocated at fixed N (`qd.root.dense(qd.i, self.n)`, per slice 145, which states fields are not resized mid-run), so a spawn/despawn count change cannot be absorbed by a `from_numpy()` upload without reallocating/recompiling fields — the design gives no mechanism. Spawn/despawn sync is explicitly in this slice's scope; "zero changes downstream" (A3) is not achievable while the snapshot and lifecycle paths read divergent CPU state.

findings.title: `_select_arch()` detects OS, not GPU availability — A7 fallback fails on a GPU-less Linux host
findings.description: `_select_arch()` returns `qd.metal` for any Darwin and `qd.cuda` for any Linux, falling back to `qd.cpu` only for a third OS. A7 (line 336) and the "no supported GPU detected … falls back to CPU" claim require actual device detection: a Linux host with no NVIDIA GPU would still select `qd.cuda` and fail at `qd.init()`/kernel launch rather than warn-and-degrade. The architecture's stated behavior ("if neither is detected it warns and falls back to `qd.cpu`") implies hardware detection, not `platform.system()`. Pin the arch to detected device availability so the advertised failsafe actually holds.

findings.title: A6 hard gate is not established as achievable on the production path
findings.description: A6 makes "≥60 TPS at N=50k on CUDA" a must-pass ship gate for the production wiring, but no evidence in the design supports it. The inherited bench baseline is 37.9 TPS at 50k (slice 145 measurements), with the ≥60 target deferred to slice 148's shared-memory tiling — which is not a declared dependency of this slice (`dependencies: ["145"]`). The production path additionally re-uploads positions every tick on wrap (the sync-back above). The parent NFR is restated correctly, but the slice should either depend on the optimization that reaches 60, provide a measurement/rationale for the production path, or reclassify A6 so it doesn't block the slice on throughput outside its control.

findings.title: GPU lifecycle boundary and config/NFR surface align with the architecture
findings.description: The new `GpuSimulationDriver` module cleanly isolates `qd.init`/field lifecycle from `SimulationManager`, matching the architecture's "clean ownership boundaries" goal and the tick-return-type contract (option a). `qd.init()` once at startup, unchanged server call site/broadcast, `ComputeConfig` added to `SimulationConfig` with parse-time validation, and the Tier 2 60-TPS-at-50k NFR restated in A6/integration test are all consistent with the parent architecture and slice plan.
